segments.text: Antarctica, from the surface down. It gets stranger every layer.
The surface. The world's largest iceberg calved in nineteen eighty six, then sat frozen to the seafloor for over thirty years before it finally drifted free.
Four kilometres down, Lake Vostok. A lake the size of Lake Ontario, sealed from sunlight for around fifteen million years.
Deeper still, an ice core pulled up ice one point two million years old. A direct record of Earth's air from before humans existed.
Under Taylor Glacier, a pocket of ancient seawater has stayed sealed for a million and a half years. It is still red, and it still has life in it, with no sunlight, ever.
And at the bottom of it all, an active volcano. Mount Erebus has held a lava lake since at least nineteen seventy two, one of only eight on Earth.
It also spits out eighty grams of gold dust a day. Antarctica has a volcano quietly raining gold, under all that ice.
